name: Tasomi-Tata
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Zur Tonlehre. Slg. hat hin und wieder Starktöne bezeichnet. Ich selbst habe die musikalischen Töne festzuhalten gesucht. Wahrscheinlich sind Starktöne und musikalische Töne in der Sprache vorhanden. Die Tonhöhen scheinen sich im Satz wenig zu verändern. Klg. hat folgende Beispiele: gya's gye sa re gya dok „der Kopf des Hundes ist klein". Hier hat gya's einfach Hochton, das sonst mit Hochtiefton von Klg. und mir notiert ist. Es ist denkbar, daß im Zusammenhang der Tiefton verloren gegangen ist; dok hat hier Tiefton, während es sonst von Klg. und mir mit Hochton gehört ist. Wahrscheinlich liegt das daran, daß das Wort hier am Satzende steht.
new_statements.translation: On tone. Seligmann [Slg.] marked stress accents (Starktöne) here and there. I myself tried to record the musical tones [pitches]. Probably both stress accents and musical tones are present in the language. The pitches seem to change little within the sentence. Klingenheben [Klg.] has the following examples: gya's gye sa re gya dok 'the dog's head is small'. Here gya's simply has high tone, which otherwise was noted with high-falling tone by Klg. and by me. It is conceivable that in connected speech the low tone was lost; dok here has low tone, whereas otherwise Klg. and I heard it with high tone. Probably this is because the word stands at the end of the sentence here.
new_statements.citation: Meinhof, Carl. 1915-1916. Sprachstudien im egyptischen Sudan. 3. Talodi. Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 6: 264-284. Berlin: Dietrich Reimer (Ernst Vohsen).
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule. Meinhof (one speaker, 1914, plus Seligmann's and Klingenheben's notes) says the language probably has both dynamic stress ('Starktöne', marked sporadically by Seligmann with an acute) and lexical pitch (high, low, high-falling tones noted on words, changing little in sentences). Where stress falls is not described by any source opened; later sources (Schadeberg 1981 via WALS 13A; Norton & Alaki 2015; Clements & Rialland 2008) treat Jomang/Talodi as a two-level tone language and say nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None; only sentence-final lowering of a word's high tone is remarked (dok high in isolation, low sentence-finally).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated words and a few short genitive sentences elicited from one speaker (Fatme of Jebel Talodi, El-Obeid 1914) plus Seligmann 1911 and Klingenheben wordlists; tone marks on citation forms; remark that pitches change little in the sentence.
new_statements.identity_note: Meinhof 1915-16 describes 'Talodi', the language of Jebel Talodi (speaker Fatme from the Talodi hill, plus Seligmann's 1910 Talodi list from Talodi/Tasume/Tata villages) = Glottolog talo1250 Tasomi-Tata (ISO tlo), called Jomang in Schadeberg 1981 and WALS (jom). Meinhof notes Nicholls' extra vocabulary may represent a different dialect. Not to be confused with the Talodi family/branch name, nor with talo1253 (Talossan, artificial).

sources.note: 'Zur Lautlehre' pp.265-267 (consonants, vowels, whispered final vowels, glottal stop) and 'Zur Tonlehre' pp.267-268: Seligmann marked 'Starktöne' (stress accents) here and there; Meinhof recorded musical tones (Hochton, Tiefton, Hochtiefton on words); 'Wahrscheinlich sind Starktöne und musikalische Töne in der Sprache vorhanden. Die Tonhöhen scheinen sich im Satz wenig zu verändern.' No statement of where stress falls; no rule.

sources.citation: WALS Online, language Jomang (jom): 13 Maddieson phonology datapoints sourced to Schadeberg 1981; 13A Tone = 'Simple tone system'; no 14A-17A stress values.
sources.note: Second-hand: codes Jomang as having a simple tone system (Schadeberg 1981); no stress features coded.

sources.citation: Bork, Ferdinand. 1913. Zu den neuen Sprachen von Süd-Kordofan. Zeitschrift für Kolonialsprachen 3: 140-156 (analysis of Seligmann's Talodi etc. lists).
sources.note: States explicitly that 'die Wirkungen des exspiratorischen und des musikalischen Akzents in diesen Sprachen [kennen wir] nicht' -- effects of stress and pitch accent in these languages are unknown.

sources.note: Tasomi-Tata data taken from Schadeberg 1981:19-46 (no fresh data); p.107: 'We omit analysis of prosodic features for lack of data and for lack of functional load...
